key_findings.finding: For influenza, primary-care/community syndromic systems are useful mainly for detecting trends and alerts rather than measuring laboratory-confirmed incidence without adjustment: Australian Flutracking symptom rates correlated significantly with laboratory notifications among unvaccinated respondents, but not vaccinated respondents, demonstrating case-definition and vaccination-related bias; the study explicitly characterized GP/hospital and laboratory surveillance as useful but incomplete.

key_findings.finding: Primary-care EHR disease estimates can have high specificity but substantial under-ascertainment when based on routine diagnostic coding. In Catalonia coeliac disease, the K90.0 code had sensitivity 91.63%, specificity 99.95%, and PPV 63.85% against laboratory/pathology review, but clinically recorded prevalence was 1.99‰ versus known seroprevalence of 5‰, indicating that coding captured diagnosed disease accurately while missing undiagnosed disease.

source_tools.relevance: Population-based primary-care coding evaluated against laboratory/pathology registries and seroprevalence reference

key_findings.finding: Completeness varies materially by disease, database, and reference standard. For prostate cancer in England, CPRD GOLD was 86% accurate/65% complete versus the cancer registry and 76%/60% versus hospital data; CPRD Aurum was 87%/77% versus the registry and 79%/70% versus hospital data. Primary-care records were often available earlier than hospital records, but linkage to registry/HES was recommended for improved case capture.

source_tools.relevance: Direct accuracy, completeness, date-concordance comparison of two primary-care EHR databases with cancer registry and HES

key_findings.finding: Validity of primary-care EHR surveillance is strongly condition- and algorithm-dependent. key_findings.finding: Overall evidence supports conditional improvement, not universal improvement, in disease-incidence estimates from primary-care surveillance.
